title: Aeron and Spark's Ribbon Mystery
markdown:
High up in the silver passes of Cloudneedle Ridge lived a young elf named Aeron. The air smelled of pine needles and starlight. Wind hummed through craggy peaks. His eyes were the colour of deepest moss after spring rain. Hair shimmered like moonlight in a cobweb. He was not a warrior, nor a grand sorcerer with a booming voice. He solved small important mysteries. He noticed. He wondered. And he had a friend, usually perched on his shoulder.

Spark was a baby dragon the size of a plump happy loaf of bread. Scales glittered like a hundred tiny amethysts. His breath was not flame but a gentle puff of smoke that smelled of toasted marshmallows. They were as close as dew on a spiderweb.

One evening the sun dipped, apricot and rose. Aeron was tidying smooth river stones when he noticed: the little lanterns lining the winding path to the Great Elder Tree were missing their ribbons. Not all, a good handful. Usually bright scarlet, neat jaunty bows. Gone, as if the wind had played a game. No breeze strong enough.

“Hmm. Where could those bright scarlet ribbons have fluttered off to?”

Spark wiggled, tilted his head, and chirped a smoky question Aeron understood.

“You think we should investigate? After dusk? When the stars are out?”

A tiny marshmallow cloud of agreement. A flutter of the good kind of nervousness, a bird testing wings. The forest at twilight was home. A puzzle waiting, the right kind of exciting for a quiet evening on the ridge.

Shy stars pricked the twilight. Fallen leaves soft underfoot. Cool sweet air, damp earth, sleeping wildflowers. No fluttery clue. Then Aeron’s keen eyes—used to beetle-gleam and moth-wing pattern—spotted a faint trail of glitter.

He touched the specks. “That’s not the sort of thing you usually find here. Moss. Pebbles. Sometimes a lost ladybug. Never glitter.”

Faint as moonbeams on water, the trail led deeper, past ancient pines huddled for warmth. Then a small rather pompous voice, trying very hard to sound important.

“Aha! Success! Another perfect incantation! The magic is strong with this one!”

Behind a moss-covered boulder big as a sleeping bear: a young wizard no older than Aeron, pointy hat wobbling, a beard almost as long as his legs. He was stacking plump red-capped mushrooms, and on each mushroom, carefully, a bright scarlet lantern ribbon.

“Excuse me. Are you the one who took the lantern ribbons?”

The wizard jumped, nearly dropped the pile. “Who dares interrupt my important work?” Chest puffed as much as a small wizard could. “I am Paloma Bumblefoot! The most brilliant young wizard in all of Cloudneedle Ridge! And yes, I have been using those ribbons for my magical research!” Research, as if a royal decree.

Spark snorted, a fizzing sparkler of unimpressed. Paloma blinked. “A dragon? It smells of sweet things. Fascinating olfactory phenomenon. But these ribbons are crucial for my spell of Mushroom Magnification. Perfectly placed for optimal magical transference.”

Aeron’s moss-green eyes twinkled. “Those are the lantern ribbons, Paloma. Everyone uses them to light their paths. They’ll be looking. Especially the little squirrels who need to find their way home.”

The proud look faltered, wobbly jelly. “Oh dear. I didn’t consider that. Spellcraft requires intense focus. Distractions are most unwelcome.” Hands wrung. Beard tickled knees.

“Magic is wonderful. Truly. But so are the simple things. Light for the path, so everyone can find their way. Perhaps there’s a way to have both?”

Paloma looked at mushrooms, at the remaining lanterns still shining bravely, back at Aeron. “A solution that doesn’t involve abandoning my spell? This will make the most magnificent giant mushrooms you have ever seen.”

“Perhaps.” Aeron glanced at Spark, who was puffing little bursts of warmth. “The moonlight is quite bright tonight. And Spark is very good at making warm glowy light.”

Spark chirped and puffed a gentle glow, not as bright as the lanterns, steady and kind.

Paloma’s eyes widened as at a new constellation. “A dragon’s natural luminosity! Of course. My spell is for magnification, not illumination. I was using the wrong kind of magic for the wrong purpose.” Beard drooped. “I was so caught up in my grand spell, I forgot the little things. The things that matter to everyone else.”

Aeron picked a scarlet ribbon from the stack and handed it back. “Sometimes the most important discoveries are the ones we overlook when we’re looking for something bigger.”

With a sincere apology and a promise to check before “using” anything else, they returned the ribbons to their lanterns. Paloma, inspired by Spark’s glow—and using a dimmer magical light of his own—cast a new spell: forest mushrooms shining with their own soft pearly light, tiny fallen stars, to guide travellers without borrowing a single bow.

Walking toward the cottage, ribbons tied and twinkling, Aeron felt a warmth like hot cocoa. Spark snuggled closer, amethyst catching starlight. They had solved the mystery, met a proud and rather funny wizard, and left the path lit two ways.

Back home, pine at the open window, a lingering whisper of marshmallow, Aeron tucked Spark into a mossy bed. A big yawn, a puff of sleep-scented smoke. Outside, the lanterns and the new mushroom-stars shared the dark, which was, for Cloudneedle Ridge, quite enough adventure for one evening.
